generatedProse.concept-context: Academic study prizes imaginative reading. A source is not just a result to record: it is an interpretation you can open up. An imaginative reader asks what a finding could mean beyond its author's own account, links it to an idea from another area, and considers a case it never tested, while staying anchored in the method and the evidence. That is analysis with imagination, not invention.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two students write about the same source and its main interpretation.

{{learner-a}} reports the interpretation accurately: this is what the author argues, and this is the evidence. The summary is correct and clear. But it stops there. {{learner-a}} records what the source says and adds nothing, so the reader learns the finding but not what to make of it.

{{learner-b}} examines the same interpretation closely, then opens it up. What else could this mean? {{learner-b}} connects it to an idea from another topic the author never mentions, and offers an original reading, still anchored in the evidence and the method. The source becomes a starting point, not a closed result.

Both students understood the source. Only {{learner-b}} read it imaginatively, making a connection of their own rather than only summarising.
generatedProse.summary: Imaginative analysis brings creativity to how you read your sources. You examine a source closely, then open it up: asking what a finding could mean, making original connections, and bringing in ideas the author never cited, while staying anchored in the method and the evidence. You can now tell an imaginative reading from a routine one and produce connections of your own. Across the course you have put creative methods to work: generating and organising ideas, thinking flexibly across approaches, and reading with imagination.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s reading more than a summary?

items.text: {{learner-b}} connected the source to another idea and produced an original reading grounded in the method and evidence.
{{learner-b}} reported the author's argument more accurately.
{{learner-b}} wrote at greater length about the source.

feedback.correct: That's right. {{learner-b}} made an original connection, grounded in the evidence, which goes beyond summarising.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} added that {{learner-a}} did not.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s reading went beyond summary because it made an original connection to another idea, anchored in the method and evidence. Accuracy, length or quotation do not.
